Let $d,N\ge1$, let $X=\mathbb R^d$, and fix macro times $t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N$. A **fine/coarse propagator pair** is a pair of deterministic maps $F_n:D_n^F\to X$ and $G_n:D_n^G\to X$, for each $0\le n<N$, where $D_n^F,D_n^G\subseteq X$ are their admitted input sets. Both maps advance a state across the same interval $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$. The labels fine and coarse identify the two roles chosen by the user; they assert no accuracy, stability, cost, or convergence property.

For an initial state $x_0\in X$, whenever every call succeeds, the **sequential fine trajectory** is the finite sequence $x_{n+1}=F_n(x_n)$, and the **sequential coarse trajectory** is defined by replacing each $F_n$ with $G_n$. A partially defined map is unavailable outside its admitted set; a failed stage evaluation or an unavailable implicit branch is a propagation failure, not a numerical value.

A canonical ODE instantiation uses the explicit Runge–Kutta stage map of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] for $r\ge1$ fine substeps of size $(t_{n+1}-t_n)/r$, composed in order to form $F_n$. A coarse backward Euler value is an endpoint $z$ satisfying the equation in [[def-backward-euler-step-equation]] over the full macro interval. Its branch selector is part of the input and must select exactly one admissible root for each admitted start state; if no such selected root exists, the coarse map is unavailable. The backward Euler definition alone asserts neither root existence nor uniqueness.

This definition distinguishes the sequential fine trajectory from samples of an exact ODE solution. Any estimate of the fine method's error relative to that exact solution is a separate obligation.

Input: an admissible propagator pair from [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]], initial state $x_0$, number of macro intervals $N$, sweep budget $K\ge0$, and optionally a wall-clock budget $\tau\ge0$ and a user-supplied convergence certificate. Each map call either returns one state or a declared failure status. The output is every fully completed row of the table $U_n^k$ for $0\le k\le K$, the last completed endpoint, and a status.

Initialize $U_0^0=x_0$ and, in increasing order of $n$, set $U_{n+1}^0=G_n(U_n^0)$. Store the values $G_n(U_n^0)$. For each $k=0,\ldots,K-1$, set $U_0^{k+1}=x_0$. Evaluate $F_n(U_n^k)$ independently for all $n$; the stored $G_n(U_n^k)$ values are reused from the preceding row. Then, in increasing order of $n$, compute $G_n(U_n^{k+1})$ and set
$$U_{n+1}^{k+1}=G_n(U_n^{k+1})+F_n(U_n^k)-G_n(U_n^k).$$
The fine calls in a sweep can run in parallel, while the corrected row is computed sequentially.

If a map call fails, return the last fully completed row and status propagation-failure; a prefix of the failed row may be reported separately but is not a completed iterate. If the time budget expires at a call boundary, return the last fully completed row and status budget-exhausted. Return status converged only if the supplied convergence certificate is verified for the returned iterate. Otherwise return status budget-exhausted when the requested initialization and $K$ sweeps finish; the procedure does not infer convergence from completion of its finite budget.

For the exact-arithmetic recurrence, an update computed with inexact fine/coarse values or an inexact correction solve can be written as the displayed right-hand side plus a combined defect $\eta_n^{k+1}$. A residual tolerance alone does not bound that defect in forward error.

**Work model.** For nonnegative call costs $c_F,c_G,\tau_{\rm sync}$ and a positive integer processor count $P$, if one fine call costs $c_F$, one coarse call costs $c_G$, and $P$ processors can evaluate independent fine calls concurrently, the initial coarse pass uses $N$ serial calls. Each completed sweep uses $N$ fine calls, with ideal fine-call span $\lceil N/P\rceil c_F$, and $N$ new coarse calls in serial order, with span $Nc_G$, plus its measured communication and synchronization cost $\tau_{\rm sync}$. The resulting idealized span is
$$Nc_G+K\bigl(\lceil N/P\rceil c_F+Nc_G+\tau_{\rm sync}\bigr).$$
This is a cost model, not a speedup guarantee; actual work, communication, processor placement, and iteration budget determine realized performance.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

For every real $x$,
$$1+x\le\exp(x).$$
Consequently, if $0\le p\le1$ and $m\in\mathbb N$, then
$$ (1-p)^m\le\exp(-mp). $$

For all real $x,y$,
$$\exp(x+y)=\exp(x)\exp(y).$$

For $x\in\mathbb R$, define
$$\exp(x):=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{x^n}{\iota(n!)}, \qquad e:=\exp(1),$$
provided by the all-real convergence proved in [[lem-exponential-series-has-infinite-radius]]. Here $n!\in\mathbb N$ is the factorial of [[def-factorial-and-falling-factorial]], $\iota(n!)$ is its nonzero real image ([[def-canonical-natural]], [[lem-of-naturals-positive]]), and powers and series are those of [[def-integer-power]] and [[def-series]].

This is a real power series centred at $0$ ([[def-real-power-series-and-radius-of-convergence]]). No logarithm, irrational power, or differential equation enters the definition.

Let $d,N\ge1$, let $\Phi_i\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ for $1\le i\le N$, and let $u_0\in\mathbb R^d$ be fixed. The linear part of a fine propagator in [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]] is represented by $\Phi_i$. For forcing vectors $g_i\in\mathbb R^d$, write the fine recurrence as $u_i=\Phi_i u_{i-1}+g_i$. On the unknown vector $v=(v_1,\ldots,v_N)\in(\mathbb R^d)^N$, define $A_t$ by $(A_tv)_1=v_1$ and $(A_tv)_i=v_i-\Phi_i v_{i-1}$ for $2\le i\le N$. With $b_1=\Phi_1u_0+g_1$ and $b_i=g_i$ for $i\ge2$, the recurrence is exactly $A_tv=b$.

For a coarsening factor $m\ge2$ dividing $N$, the coarse indices are $0,m,2m,\ldots,N$. Among unknowns, let $C=\{m,2m,\ldots,N\}$ and $F=\{1,\ldots,N\}\setminus C$. Reordering the unknown vector as $(v_F,v_C)$ gives
$$A_t=\begin{pmatrix}A_{FF}&A_{FC}\\ A_{CF}&A_{CC}\end{pmatrix}.$$
A practical coarse propagator $\Psi_j$ on each interval is the linear subcase of the coarse maps $G_n$ in [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]]; the exact coarse operator is determined by eliminating F-points and is not generally the same as this practical choice. This definition asserts no stability or convergence property.

derivations.claim: For any right-hand side, solve the fine equations in increasing index: the first unknown is determined by its identity diagonal block, and each later unknown is uniquely $u_i=r_i+\Phi_i u_{i-1}$. This proves $A_t$ is invertible. Holding all C-values fixed, the F-equations in each interval between consecutive C-points have the same forward-substitution form with identity diagonal blocks, so they uniquely determine the F-values; hence $A_{FF}$ is invertible.

In the reordered block system, the F rows give $u_F=A_{FF}^{-1}(b_F-A_{FC}u_C)$. Substituting this expression in the C rows gives $(A_{CC}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC})u_C=b_C-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}b_F$. Conversely, any solution $u_C$ of this coarse system, together with the displayed formula for $u_F$, satisfies both the F and C rows. Thus elimination preserves exactly the solution set.

Repeated substitution in $u_i=\Phi_i u_{i-1}+g_i$, for $i=(j-1)m+1,\ldots,jm$, gives $u_{jm}=(\Phi_{jm}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+1})u_{(j-1)m}+\sum_{s=1}^{m}(\Phi_{jm}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+s+1})g_{(j-1)m+s}$. For $s=m$ the product is empty and equals $I$. This is exactly the coarse recurrence in the Statement; the coefficient product reduces to $\Phi^m$ when every $\Phi_i=\Phi$.

Let $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^n$ be open, let $F:D\to\mathbb R^n$, and let $n\ge1$. The equation

$$x'(t)=F(t,x(t))$$

is a **first-order system**. An **initial value problem** consists of this equation and data $(t_0,x_0)\in D$, written $x(t_0)=x_0$.

A **solution on an interval** $I$ is a function $x:I\to\mathbb R^n$ such that $t_0\in I$, $(t,x(t))\in D$ for every $t\in I$, $x$ is differentiable on $I$ in the domain-relative sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]], and

$$x(t_0)=x_0,\qquad x'(t)=F(t,x(t))\quad(t\in I).$$

Endpoints of $I$ use the corresponding one-sided, domain-relative derivative. A local solution is one whose interval contains a nondegenerate neighborhood of $t_0$ relative to the time projection of $D$.

Let $d,N\ge1$, let $X=\mathbb R^d$, and fix macro times $t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N$. A **fine/coarse propagator pair** is a pair of deterministic maps $F_n:D_n^F\to X$ and $G_n:D_n^G\to X$, for each $0\le n<N$, where $D_n^F,D_n^G\subseteq X$ are their admitted input sets. Both maps advance a state across the same interval $[t_n,t_{n+1}]$. The labels fine and coarse identify the two roles chosen by the user; they assert no accuracy, stability, cost, or convergence property.

For an initial state $x_0\in X$, whenever every call succeeds, the **sequential fine trajectory** is the finite sequence $x_{n+1}=F_n(x_n)$, and the **sequential coarse trajectory** is defined by replacing each $F_n$ with $G_n$. A partially defined map is unavailable outside its admitted set; a failed stage evaluation or an unavailable implicit branch is a propagation failure, not a numerical value.

A canonical ODE instantiation uses the explicit Runge–Kutta stage map of [[def-explicit-runge-kutta-tableau-and-stage-map]] for $r\ge1$ fine substeps of size $(t_{n+1}-t_n)/r$, composed in order to form $F_n$. A coarse backward Euler value is an endpoint $z$ satisfying the equation in [[def-backward-euler-step-equation]] over the full macro interval. Its branch selector is part of the input and must select exactly one admissible root for each admitted start state; if no such selected root exists, the coarse map is unavailable. The backward Euler definition alone asserts neither root existence nor uniqueness.

This definition distinguishes the sequential fine trajectory from samples of an exact ODE solution. Any estimate of the fine method's error relative to that exact solution is a separate obligation.

Use the notation and Lipschitz hypotheses of [[thm-parareal-binomial-error-bound]], with $A=\max\{1,a\}$. Let computed iterates $V_n^k$ satisfy $V_0^k=x_0$, $\|V_n^0-x_n\|\le M$, and, for each requested correction,
$$\left\|V_{n+1}^{k+1}-\left[G_n(V_n^{k+1})+(F_n-G_n)(V_n^k)\right]\right\|\le\eta$$
for a constant $\eta\ge0$. Define $P_n^k=M\binom nk A^n b^k$ and a nonnegative forcing array by $R_0^k=0$, $R_n^0=0$, and
$$R_{n+1}^{k+1}=A R_n^{k+1}+bR_n^k+\eta.$$
Then $\|V_n^k-x_n\|\le P_n^k+R_n^k$ for every completed node and sweep.

The base envelope $M$ includes coarse-initialization error relative to the fine trajectory. The per-update defect $\eta$ must bound the actual combined effect of fine/coarse evaluation errors and correction-solve error; a residual tolerance alone supplies no forward-error bound.

Input: a linear fine-grid system $A_tu=b$ with $N\ge1$ fine intervals as in [[def-linear-all-at-once-time-operator]], a coarsening factor $m\ge2$ dividing $N$ and its C/F partition as in [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]], practical coarse propagators $\Psi_j\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ for $1\le j\le N_c:=N/m$, an initial fine-grid iterate $u_{\rm in}$, pre- and post-relaxation choices from $\{F,FCF\}$, a real-valued norm on the fine-grid residual space as in [[def-norm-and-normed-space]], a nonnegative integer cycle budget $J_{\rm cyc}$, and a residual tolerance $\varepsilon\ge0$. The symbol $J_{\rm cyc}$ is the number of permitted cycles; the coarse-interval count is $N_c$ (the letter $J$ in [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]] denotes that lemma's coarse-interval count). The output is the last iterate, its residual norm, the number of completed cycles, and status `converged` or `budget-exhausted`.

In F/C ordering define ideal interpolation $P$ and restriction $R$ by
$$P=\begin{bmatrix}-A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC}\\ I_C\end{bmatrix},
\qquad R=\begin{bmatrix}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}&I_C\end{bmatrix}.$$

The exact coarse operator is the Schur complement $RA_tP=A_{CC}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC}$ from [[lem-mgrit-exact-coarse-elimination]]. The practical correction matrix $A_c$ has identity diagonal blocks and subdiagonal blocks $-\Psi_j$ for $2\le j\le N_c$; its first row corresponds to the fixed zero initial correction $z_0=0$. For any right-hand side $\rho$, forward substitution uniquely solves $A_cz=\rho$ by setting $z_0=0$ and, in increasing order for $j=1,\ldots,N_c$, setting $z_j=\rho_j+\Psi_jz_{j-1}$. Thus $A_c$ is invertible even when an individual $\Psi_j$ is singular.

Define the relaxations on $A_tu=b$ as follows. An F-relaxation holds every C-value fixed and, for each coarse interval $j=1,\ldots,N_c$, updates its F-indices $i=(j-1)m+1,\ldots,jm-1$ in increasing order: set $u_1=b_1$ if $i=1$, and otherwise set $u_i=b_i+\Phi_i u_{i-1}$. Different coarse intervals have independent F-updates and may be processed in parallel. A C-relaxation holds every F-value fixed and, for $j=1,\ldots,N_c$ in increasing order, sets $u_{jm}=b_{jm}+\Phi_{jm}u_{jm-1}$; these C-updates are independent because $m\ge2$ and each predecessor is an F-index. An FCF-relaxation applies F-relaxation, then C-relaxation, then F-relaxation. Each relaxation is a finite linear update; write $S_{\rm pre}$ and $S_{\rm post}$ for the error maps of the selected pre- and post-relaxations.

For one cycle from a current iterate $u$, apply the selected pre-relaxation; form $r=b-A_tu$ and $\rho=Rr$; solve $A_cz=\rho$ by the forward substitution above; correct $u\leftarrow u+Pz$; then apply the selected post-relaxation. The exact error-propagation matrix of this fixed cycle is
$$E=S_{\rm post}(I-PA_c^{-1}RA_t)S_{\rm pre}.$$

Initialize $u^{(0)}=u_{\rm in}$ and compute $\|b-A_tu^{(0)}\|$. If this is at most $\varepsilon$, return $u^{(0)}$, zero completed cycles, and status `converged`. Otherwise, for $j_{\rm cyc}=1,\ldots,J_{\rm cyc}$, perform one cycle, call the resulting iterate $u^{(j_{\rm cyc})}$, and compute $\|b-A_tu^{(j_{\rm cyc})}\|$. If this norm is at most $\varepsilon$, return that iterate, $j_{\rm cyc}$ completed cycles, and status `converged`; if not, continue. If all $J_{\rm cyc}$ cycles finish without this condition (including when $J_{\rm cyc}=0$), return the last iterate, its residual norm, and status `budget-exhausted`. The matrix $E$ describes exact arithmetic and exact coarse solves; inexact solves contribute an update defect that needs its own bound.

**Work model.** Let $N_f=N$ and $N_c=N/m$. One F-relaxation updates $N_f-N_c$ F-points, but its boundary assignment $u_1=b_1$ uses the supplied right-hand side and makes no fine-propagator call; thus it uses $N_f-N_c-1$ fine-propagator calls; one C-relaxation uses $N_c$ fine-propagator calls, one for each C equation; one FCF-relaxation uses $2(N_f-N_c-1)+N_c$ fine-propagator calls. Residual formation and ideal interpolation add their actual fine-propagator applications and communication when recomputed rather than cached. The specified coarse forward substitution uses $N_c$ practical coarse-propagator applications, including $\Psi_1z_0$ with $z_0=0$. If a fine call costs $c_\Phi$, a coarse call costs $c_\Psi$, and $p_{\rm proc}$ processors share independent F-intervals (the interpolation matrix remains $P$), work is the sum of these calls and communication, while span includes the sequential dependence within each F-interval, the coarse forward solve, and synchronization. A multilevel cycle adds the work and span on every visited level. This model gives no speedup guarantee.

Use [[def-linear-all-at-once-time-operator]] with $N=Jm$, $m\ge2$, and its F/C partition. Both $A_t$ and $A_{FF}$ are invertible. Eliminating the F unknowns from $A_tv=b$ gives the coarse system with Schur complement
$$S=A_{CC}-A_{CF}A_{FF}^{-1}A_{FC}.$$
On coarse interval $j$, its recurrence is
$$u_{jm}-(\Phi_{jm}\Phi_{jm-1}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+1})u_{(j-1)m}=\bar g_j,$$
where
$$\bar g_j=\sum_{s=1}^{m}(\Phi_{jm}\Phi_{jm-1}\cdots\Phi_{(j-1)m+s+1})g_{(j-1)m+s},$$
with an empty product defined to be the identity. If $\Phi_i=\Phi$ for every fine step, the exact coarse propagator is $\Phi^m$.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

Let $f:D\to\mathbb R^d$ define a first-order initial-value problem on an open time-state domain $D\subseteq\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^d$. Given a time $t_n$, step $h_n>0$, and state $y_n$ with $(t_n,y_n)\in D$, an admissible endpoint $y_{n+1}$ must satisfy $(t_n+h_n,y_{n+1})\in D$. The backward Euler endpoint is any such $y_{n+1}$ satisfying

$$y_{n+1}=y_n+h_n f(t_n+h_n,y_{n+1}).$$

Its update residual at an approximate endpoint $z$ with $(t_n+h_n,z)\in D$ is

$$G_n^{\rm BE}(z)=z-y_n-h_n f(t_n+h_n,z).$$

When $f$ is defined at the endpoint, the derivative residual is $G_n^{\rm BE}(z)/h_n$. The equation can have no, one, or several roots on a restricted admissible branch set; this definition by itself asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Input: an admissible propagator pair from [[def-parareal-propagator-pair]], initial state $x_0$, number of macro intervals $N$, sweep budget $K\ge0$, and optionally a wall-clock budget $\tau\ge0$ and a user-supplied convergence certificate. Each map call either returns one state or a declared failure status. The output is every fully completed row of the table $U_n^k$ for $0\le k\le K$, the last completed endpoint, and a status.

Initialize $U_0^0=x_0$ and, in increasing order of $n$, set $U_{n+1}^0=G_n(U_n^0)$. Store the values $G_n(U_n^0)$. For each $k=0,\ldots,K-1$, set $U_0^{k+1}=x_0$. Evaluate $F_n(U_n^k)$ independently for all $n$; the stored $G_n(U_n^k)$ values are reused from the preceding row. Then, in increasing order of $n$, compute $G_n(U_n^{k+1})$ and set
$$U_{n+1}^{k+1}=G_n(U_n^{k+1})+F_n(U_n^k)-G_n(U_n^k).$$
The fine calls in a sweep can run in parallel, while the corrected row is computed sequentially.

The backward Euler endpoint is any such $y_{n+1}$ satisfying

$$y_{n+1}=y_n+h_n f(t_n+h_n,y_{n+1}).$$

Its update residual at an approximate endpoint $z$ with $(t_n+h_n,z)\in D$ is

$$G_n^{\rm BE}(z)=z-y_n-h_n f(t_n+h_n,z).$$

When $f$ is defined at the endpoint, the derivative residual is $G_n^{\rm BE}(z)/h_n$. The equation can have no, one, or several roots on a restricted admissible branch set; this definition by itself asserts neither existence nor uniqueness.

Throughout this page $\mathbb{R}$ is the complete ordered field
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]) constructed in this library, in particular a
field, so that "vector space" below always means vector space over $\mathbb{R}$
([[def-vector-space]]).

Let $V$ be a vector space over $\mathbb{R}$, with zero vector $0_V$. A **norm on
$V$** is a function $N : V \to \mathbb{R}$ such that for all $u, v \in V$ and all
$\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **(N1) Separation.** $N(v) = 0$ if and only if $v = 0_V$.
- **(N2) Absolute homogeneity.** $N(\lambda v) = |\lambda|\,N(v)$, the absolute
  value being that of [[def-abs-value]].
- **(N3) Triangle inequality.** $N(u + v) \le N(u) + N(v)$.

A **normed space** is a pair $(V, N)$ consisting of a vector space $V$ over
$\mathbb{R}$ and a norm $N$ on it. When only one norm is in play we write
$\lVert v\rVert$ for $N(v)$; when several are, the norm is always named.

**The values of a norm are real numbers.** The codomain is $\mathbb{R}$, so
$N(v)$ is an honest element of the complete ordered field and no infinite value
is permitted. The same real-valued codomain is required of a metric by
[[def-metric-space]].

### Nonnegativity is a theorem, not an axiom

Many texts add a fourth condition $N(v) \ge 0$. It is redundant. Applying (N2)
with $\lambda = -1$ gives $N(-v) = |-1|\,N(v) = N(v)$ ([[lem-of-abs-value]],
[[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]] for $(-1)v = -v$), and then (N3)
with $u = v$ and $-v$ gives

$$0 \;=\; N(0_V) \;=\; N\bigl(v + (-v)\bigr) \;\le\; N(v) + N(-v) \;=\; N(v) + N(v),$$

where $N(0_V) = 0$ is (N1). So $N(v) + N(v) \ge 0$, and if $N(v) < 0$ then
$N(v) + N(v) < 0$ by addition of inequalities, which trichotomy forbids
([[def-complete-ordered-field]]). Hence $N(v) \ge 0$ for every $v \in V$.

**Consequently the verification of a candidate norm has three things to check and
not four**, exactly as the verification of a candidate metric has three and not
four ([[def-metric-space]], [[lem-metric-nonnegativity]]). No item in this
library assumes nonnegativity of a norm before the argument above.

### The induced metric

Let $N$ be a norm on $V$ and define

$$d_N(u,v) \;:=\; N(u - v) \qquad (u, v \in V),$$

where $u - v = u + (-v)$ ([[def-vector-space]]). **Then $d_N$ is a metric on
$V$** ([[def-metric-space]]), and the three axioms are the three conditions
above, in order:

- **(M1)** $d_N(u,v) = 0$ means $N(u-v) = 0$, which by (N1) says $u - v = 0_V$,
  that is $u = v$; and conversely $d_N(v,v) = N(0_V) = 0$.
- **(M2)** $d_N(v,u) = N(v-u) = N\bigl((-1)(u-v)\bigr) = |-1|\,N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$,
  by (N2), [[lem-of-abs-value]] and $(-1)w = -w$
  ([[lem-vector-space-elementary-consequences]]).
- **(M3)** $d_N(u,w) = N\bigl((u-v) + (v-w)\bigr) \le N(u-v) + N(v-w) = d_N(u,v) + d_N(v,w)$,
  by (N3).

A normed space is therefore a metric space, and every notion defined for metric
spaces — open set ([[def-metric-topology]]), convergence, Cauchyness,
continuity, compactness — is available in it with no further definition. **This
library never introduces a second notion of any of them for normed spaces.**

### Two properties an arbitrary metric need not have

The metric $d_N$ satisfies, for all $u, v, w \in V$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$:

- **translation invariance**, $d_N(u + w, v + w) = N\bigl((u+w)-(v+w)\bigr) = N(u-v) = d_N(u,v)$;
- **absolute homogeneity**, $d_N(\lambda u, \lambda v) = N\bigl(\lambda(u-v)\bigr) = |\lambda|\,d_N(u,v)$, by (N2).

**Not every metric on a vector space arises from a norm**, and homogeneity is
what fails. The published bounded remetrisation [[lem-bounded-remetrisation]]
replaces a metric $d$ by $d' = \min\{d, 1\}$, a metric with the same topology
whose values never exceed $1$; on a vector space $V$ containing a vector $v$ with
$d(v, 0_V) > 0$ this $d'$ cannot be $d_M$ for any norm $M$, since absolute
homogeneity would force $d'(\lambda v, 0_V) = |\lambda|\,d'(v, 0_V)$, which is
unbounded in $\lambda$, while $d'$ is bounded by $1$. So the passage from norms
to metrics is not reversible, and a statement about a metric on a vector space is
strictly weaker than the corresponding statement about a norm.

In fine order the error operator is $A_t=\begin{pmatrix}1&0&0&0\\-\alpha&1&0&0\\0&-\alpha&1&0\\0&0&-\alpha&1\end{pmatrix}$. In F/C order $F=(1,3)$, $C=(2,4)$, its blocks are $A_{FF}=I$, $A_{FC}=\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\-\alpha&0\end{pmatrix}$, $A_{CF}=\begin{pmatrix}-\alpha&0\\0&-\alpha\end{pmatrix}$, and $A_{CC}=I$. Hence [F4] gives $S=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-\alpha^2&1\end{pmatrix}$.

F-relaxation maps an error $(e_1,e_2,e_3,e_4)$ to $(0,e_2,\alpha e_2,e_4)$, so the F-row residuals vanish and the ideal restriction in [F5] reduces to the C residual $(e_2,e_4-\alpha^2e_2)$. Solving the practical coarse system $\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\-\psi&1\end{pmatrix}z=(e_2,e_4-\alpha^2e_2)$ gives $z_1=e_2$, $z_2=e_4+(\psi-\alpha^2)e_2$. Subtracting the ideal interpolation [F5] leaves $(0,0,0,(\alpha^2-\psi)e_2)$; post-F-relaxation leaves this vector unchanged.

Therefore $E$ has its only nonzero entry in row $4$, column $2$, equal to $\alpha^2-\psi=\frac9{16}-\frac23=-\frac5{48}$. For the norm in [A1], $\|Ee\|_\infty=\frac5{48}|e_2|\le\frac5{48}\|e\|_\infty$, with equality when $e=(0,1,0,0)$. Thus $\|E\|_\infty=5/48<1$.

For every $e\in\mathbb R^4$, $\|e\|_\infty=\max_i|e_i|$ is nonnegative and vanishes only when every coordinate is zero; $\|\lambda e\|_\infty=|\lambda|\|e\|_\infty$; and $\|e+f\|_\infty\le\|e\|_\infty+\|f\|_\infty$. Thus the norm in [A1] satisfies [F7]. For any matrix $B$, $\|Bv\|_\infty\le(\max_i\sum_j|B_{ij}|)\|v\|_\infty$ by applying the finite triangle inequality to each row. The row sums of $A_t$ are at most $1+\alpha=7/4$. If $A_tu=w$, forward substitution gives $u_1=w_1$ and $u_i=w_i+\alpha u_{i-1}$, hence by induction $u_i=\sum_{j=1}^{i}\alpha^{i-j}w_j$. Therefore $A_t^{-1}$ has entries $\alpha^{i-j}$ for $i\ge j$ and zero otherwise, with row sums at most $1+\alpha+\alpha^2+\alpha^3=175/64$. Thus $\|A_t\|_\infty\le7/4$ and $\|A_t^{-1}\|_\infty\le175/64$. All hypotheses of [F6] hold with $q=5/48$, so the error after $r$ cycles is at most $(5/48)^r$ times its initial value.
